body_md: A logic $\ensuremath{\mathrm L}$ in a language $\ensuremath{\mathcal L} \supseteq \ensuremath{\mathcal L}_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm {Ab}}}}$ is \emph{superabelian} if\/ $\ensuremath{\mathrm L}$ is an expansion of ${\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm {Ab}}}}$ satisfying \ensuremath{\mathrm{(sCNG_{\mathit c})}} for each $c \in \ensuremath{\mathcal L} \setminus \ensuremath{\mathcal L}_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm {Ab}}}}$.

title: Definition
body_md:
A superabelian logic $\ensuremath{\mathrm L}$ enjoys the {\em (Finite) Strong ${{\mathbb K}}$-Completeness} with respect to a class ${{\mathbb K}}$ of $\ensuremath{\mathrm L}$-algebras, $\mathrm{(F)}${\ensuremath{\mathrm{S}{{\mathbb K}}\mathrm{C}}}\ for short, if for every (finite) set $\Gamma\cup\{\ensuremath{\varphi}\}$ of formulas,
$$
\Gamma \vdash_\ensuremath{\mathrm L} \ensuremath{\varphi}\qquad \text{iff}\qquad \Gamma \vDash_{{\mathbb K}} \ensuremath{\varphi}.
$$

body_md: A superabelian logic $\ensuremath{\mathrm L}$ is \emph{semilinear} if it has the Strong $\mathbf{Alg}^{\ell}(\ensuremath{\mathrm L})$-Completeness.

title: Definition
body_md:
The lattice connective $\lor$ is a \emph{strong disjunction} in a superabelian logic $\ensuremath{\mathrm L}$ if for each set  $\Gamma \cup\Phi\cup \Psi \cup \{\xi\}$ of formulas,
$$\frac{\Gamma,\Phi\vdash_\ensuremath{\mathrm L}\xi\qquad \Gamma,\Psi\vdash_\ensuremath{\mathrm L}\xi}{\Gamma,\Phi\lor \Psi\vdash_\ensuremath{\mathrm L}\xi},$$
 where $\Phi\lor \Psi$ is short for $\{\ensuremath{\varphi} \lor \ensuremath{\psi} \mid \ensuremath{\varphi} \in \Phi, \ensuremath{\psi} \in \Psi\}.$

title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{t:equivalence_disj_semilinearity}
Let \ensuremath{\mathrm L} be a superabelian logic with a countable presentation. Then, $\ensuremath{\mathrm L}$ is semilinear iff $\lor$ is a strong disjunction.

title: Definition
body_md: Let $\Gamma \cup \{\varphi\} \subseteq  \ensuremath{\mathit{Fm}_{\!\ensuremath{\mathcal L}}}$. The \emph{$\lor$-form} of\/ a consecution $\Gamma \mathrel{\blacktriangleright} \ensuremath{\varphi}$ is the set of the consecutions $$(\Gamma \mathrel{\blacktriangleright} \ensuremath{\varphi}) ^\lor=\{\Gamma \lor \ensuremath{\psi} \mathrel{\blacktriangleright} \ensuremath{\varphi} \lor \ensuremath{\psi} \mid \ensuremath{\psi} \in \ensuremath{\mathit{Fm}_{\!\ensuremath{\mathcal L}}}\}.$$

label: l:about nabla-forms
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Take an evaluation $e$ such that, for each $\xi \in \Gamma$, we have $e(\xi) \geq 0$. Then clearly $e(\xi \lor \ensuremath{\varphi}) \geq 0$ (${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$ has a lattice reduct). Thus by our assumption for $\ensuremath{\psi}=\ensuremath{\varphi}$, we know that $e(\ensuremath{\varphi}) = e(\ensuremath{\varphi} \lor \ensuremath{\varphi}) \geq 0$.
	
For the converse implication, take an evaluation $e$ such that $e(\xi \lor \ensuremath{\psi}) \geq 0$ for each $\xi \in \Gamma$. Since we assume that ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$ is linearly ordered, we can derive that either $e(\ensuremath{\psi})  \geq 0$ or, for all $\xi \in \Gamma$, we have $e(\xi) \geq 0$.
In the latter case, the assumption $\Gamma \vDash_{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}} \ensuremath{\varphi}$ gives us $e(\ensuremath{\varphi})  \geq 0$ and so in both cases we have $e(\ensuremath{\varphi} \lor \ensuremath{\psi})  \geq 0$.

label: t:semilinearity of Ab
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{t:semilinearity of Ab}
${\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm {Ab}}}}$ is a semilinear logic with strong disjunction $\vee$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
As ${\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm {Ab}}}}$ has a countable presentation, it suffices to prove that $\vee$ is a strong disjunction which, thanks to~Theorem~\ref{t:strong disjunction}, follows if we prove that ${\ensuremath{\mathrm{(Adj)}}}^\lor$ and ${\ensuremath{\mathrm{(MP)}}}^\lor$ are valid in ${\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm {Ab}}}}$.

For the first one, let {\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}\ be an Abelian $\ell$-group and $e$ an ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$-evaluation such that $e(\ensuremath{\varphi} \lor \xi) \geq 0$ and $e(\ensuremath{\psi} \lor \xi) \geq 0$. Then, by the assumptions and distributivity of the lattice operations, we have:
$$
e((\ensuremath{\varphi} \land \ensuremath{\psi}) \lor \xi) = e((\ensuremath{\varphi} \lor \xi) \land (\ensuremath{\psi} \lor \xi)) = e(\ensuremath{\varphi} \lor \xi) \land e(\ensuremath{\psi} \lor \xi)
\geq 0.
$$

To prove the validity of ${\ensuremath{\mathrm{(MP)}}}^\lor$, consider an evaluation $e$ such that $0 \leq e(\ensuremath{\varphi} \lor \xi)$ and  $0 \leq e((\ensuremath{\varphi} \rightarrow \ensuremath{\psi}) \lor \xi)$. This gives us $0=e(\ensuremath{\varphi} \lor \xi) \land 0=e((\ensuremath{\varphi} \rightarrow \ensuremath{\psi}) \lor \xi) \land 0$. Using the distributivity of the lattice operations, we obtain 
$$
0=e((\ensuremath{\varphi} \land \ensuremath{\mathtt{t}}) \lor (\xi \land \ensuremath{\mathtt{t}})) = e(((\ensuremath{\varphi} \rightarrow \ensuremath{\psi})  \land \ensuremath{\mathtt{t}}) \lor (\xi \land \ensuremath{\mathtt{t}})).
$$
For simplicity, let us set $e(\ensuremath{\varphi} \land \ensuremath{\mathtt{t}}) = a$, $e(\ensuremath{\psi}) = b$, $e(\xi \land \ensuremath{\mathtt{t}}) = c$ and $e((\ensuremath{\varphi}\rightarrow \ensuremath{\psi})  \land \ensuremath{\mathtt{t}})=d$. As in $\ell$-groups it holds $(a \lor b) + c= (a+c) \lor (b+c)$, we obtain
$$
0=(a \lor c)+(d \lor c)=(a+d) \lor (a+c) \lor (c+d) \lor (2c). 
$$
Note that, due to monotonicity of addition, we have 
\begin{align*}
a+d & \leq e(\ensuremath{\varphi})+ (e(\ensuremath{\varphi}) \rightarrow e(\ensuremath{\psi}) ) = b\\
(a+c) \lor (c+d) \lor (2c) & \leq  (0 + c)\vee (c+ 0) \vee (c+0)\leq c.
\end{align*}
Therefore, we obtain $0 \leq b \lor c=e(\ensuremath{\psi}) \lor e(\xi \wedge \ensuremath{\mathtt{t}}) \leq e(\ensuremath{\psi} \lor \xi)$ as required.

label: c:semilinearity_criterium
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{c:semilinearity_criterium}
Let $\ensuremath{\mathrm L}$ be a superabelian logic expanding ${\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm {Ab}}}}$ by a set $\mathcal{S}$ of consecutions such that $R^\lor$ is valid in $\ensuremath{\mathrm L}$ for each $R \in \mathcal{S}$. Then, $\vee$ is a strong disjunction in~$\ensuremath{\mathrm L}$. If, furthermore, $\ensuremath{\mathrm L}$ has a countable presentation, then $\ensuremath{\mathrm L}$ is semilinear.

The variety $\mathbb{AL}$ of Abelian $\ell$-groups is generated (as a quasivariety) by any of its  non-trivial members, that is, $\ensuremath{\mathbf{ISPP}}_\mathrm{U}({\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}})=\mathbb{AL}$ for any non-trivial ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}} \in \mathbb{AL}$. title: Definition
body_md:
Let ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$ be an Abelian $\ell$-group. We say ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$ is Archimedean if and only if for each $a,b \in A$ it holds:
$$(\forall n \in \mathbb N) \; na\leq b \implies  a \leq 0.$$
head: environment

title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We first show the implication from 1 to 2.
Let $e$ be an evaluation such that we have $e(\ensuremath{\varphi}) \ngeq 0$. We set $a=-e(\ensuremath{\varphi})$ and $b=-e(\ensuremath{\psi})$.
Since ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$ is Archimedean and $a\nleq 0$, there is an $n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$ such that $n \cdot a \nleq b$. Consequently, there is an $n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$ such that
$n \cdot e(\ensuremath{\varphi})  \ngeq e(\ensuremath{\psi}) $; thus $e(\ensuremath{\psi} \rightarrow n \cdot \ensuremath{\varphi}) \ngeq 0$. This shows that \ensuremath{\mathrm{(Arch)}} holds.

To show the implication from 2 to 1, we assume that ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$ is not Archimedean. Therefore, there exist $a,b \in A$ such that $a \nleq 0$ and $n \cdot a \leq b$ for each $n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$. Consider an evaluation $e$ such that $e(\ensuremath{\varphi})=-a$ and $e(\ensuremath{\psi})=-b$. Then, for each $n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$, we have $n \cdot e(\ensuremath{\varphi}) \geq e(\ensuremath{\psi})$ and thus $e(\ensuremath{\psi} \rightarrow n \cdot \ensuremath{\varphi}) \geq 0$ for each $n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$. However, by assumption, $e(\ensuremath{\varphi})=-a \ngeq 0$ and thus \ensuremath{\mathrm{(Arch)}} fails in ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$.

The rest of the statement follows from Lemma~\ref{l:about nabla-forms}.

label: e:ArchNonArch
title: Example
body_md:
\label{e:ArchNonArch}
Clearly the algebras $\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{R}}}}}$, $\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Q}}}}}$, and $\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Z}}}}}$ are Archimedean. 
As an example of a non-Archimedean linearly ordered $\ell$-group, consider the lexicographic product of two copies of the integers $\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Z}}}}} \times_{\text{lex}} \ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Z}}}}}$, where $\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Z}}}}} \times_{\text{lex}} \ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Z}}}}}$ has the same group structure as $\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Z}}}}} \times \ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Z}}}}}$, with the ordering $\ensuremath{\langle{a,b}\rangle} > \ensuremath{\langle{c,d}\rangle}$ iff $a>c$ or $a=c$ and $b >d$.
This $\ell$-group is clearly not Archimedean, since by definition $n \cdot \ensuremath{\langle{0,1}\rangle}<\ensuremath{\langle{1,0}\rangle}$ for each $n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$.

title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{t:realAbel}
${\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm {rAb}}}}$ is the extension of ${\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm {Ab}}}}$ by the rule $\ensuremath{\mathrm{(Arch)}}^\lor\!$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Let us denote the logic ${\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm {Ab}}}}+\ensuremath{\mathrm{(Arch)}}^\lor\!$ by $\ensuremath{\mathrm L}$. First note that, by Corollary~\ref{c:semilinearity_criterium}, we know that $\ensuremath{\mathrm L}$ is a semilinear logic and so it is strongly complete with respect to the class $\mathbf{Alg}^{\ell}(\ensuremath{\mathrm L})$, which, due to the previous lemma, consists of linearly ordered Archimedean $\ell$-groups. By Hölder's Theorem~\cite{Holder:Axiome}, each such $\ell$-group is embeddable into $\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{R}}}}}$ and so the proof follows.

label: p:irrational
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{p:irrational}
Given $0<\gamma \in \ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{R}}}}} \setminus \ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Q}}}}}$, a sequence of rationals $\ensuremath{\langle{q_j}\rangle}_{j \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}}$ strictly increasing and converging to $\gamma$, and a sequence of rationals $\ensuremath{\langle{r_j}\rangle}_{j \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}}$ strictly decreasing and converging to $\gamma$,
the logic ${\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm {rAb}}}}+\ensuremath{\mathrm{(str_\gamma)}}^\lor$ is strongly complete w.r.t.\ 
$${{\mathbb K}}=\{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}} \subseteq \ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{R}}}}} \mid (\forall a,b \in A) \;  (b=  \gamma \cdot a \implies a=0) \}.$$
Moreover, for any ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}} \in \ensuremath{\mathbf{IS}}(\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{R}}}}})$ we have ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}} \vDash \ensuremath{\mathrm{(str_\gamma)}}^\lor$ if and only if ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}} \in {{\mathbb K}}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since the logic ${\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm {rAb}}}}+\ensuremath{\mathrm{(str_\gamma)}}^\lor$ satisfies the conditions from Corollary~\ref{c:semilinearity_criterium}, it is semilinear. Since ${\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm {rAb}}}}+\ensuremath{\mathrm{(str_\gamma)}}^\lor$ is an extension of ${\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm {rAb}}}}$, we obtain that ${\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm {rAb}}}}+\ensuremath{\mathrm{(str_\gamma)}}^\lor$ is strongly complete w.r.t.\ some subclass of $\ensuremath{\mathbf{S}}(\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{R}}}}})$.  


    We need the following technical observation:
    \begin{obs}
       Let ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}} \subseteq \ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{R}}}}}$ and $a,b \in A$.
       Then we have:
       $$ q_j \cdot a \leq b \text{ and } b \leq r_j \cdot a \text{ for each } j \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}} \iff b=\gamma \cdot a \text{ and }a \geq 0.$$
    \end{obs}
    \begin{proofmiddle}
        First, since $q_0 \cdot a \leq b \leq r_0 \cdot a$ and $q_0 < r_0$, we can conclude that $0 \leq a$. 
        We have $\lim q_j=\gamma$ and $\lim r_j=\gamma$. Consequently, $\gamma \cdot a=\lim q_j \cdot a \leq b \leq \lim r_j \cdot a=\gamma \cdot a$. Therefore, we obtain $\gamma \cdot a=b$. The other direction follows as well: if $\gamma \cdot a=b$ and $a \geq 0$, then $q_j \cdot a \leq \gamma \cdot a=b$ for each $j \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$ (since $a \geq 0$ and $q_j$ is strictly increasing) and $b=\gamma \cdot a \leq r_j \cdot a$ for each $j \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$ (since $a \geq 0$ and $r_j$ is strictly decreasing).
    \end{proofmiddle}
  
First, let us take an arbitrary ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}} \in \mathbb K$.
     We show that ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$ satisfies $\ensuremath{\mathrm{(str_\gamma)}}^\lor$. 
     By the observation and the definition of ${{\mathbb K}}$, if, for $a,b \in A$, we have $q_j \cdot a \leq b$ and $b \leq r_j \cdot a$ for each $j \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$, then it must be that $a=0$. Thus, any evaluation in ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$ that satisfies the premise of $\ensuremath{\mathrm{(str_\gamma)}}$ must map $\ensuremath{\varphi}$ to $0$, thereby satisfying the conclusion $\ensuremath{\varphi} \rightarrow \ensuremath{\mathtt{t}}$. Therefore, $\ensuremath{\mathrm{(str_\gamma)}}$ is valid in ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$. Since ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$ is a chain, by Lemma~\ref{l:about nabla-forms} $\ensuremath{\mathrm{(str_\gamma)}}^{\lor}$ is also valid in ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$, and thus ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$ is a model of ${\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm {rAb}}}}+\ensuremath{\mathrm{(str_\gamma)}}^\lor$.

    To prove the other direction, assume for an algebra ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{1}}}} \neq {\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}} \subseteq \ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{R}}}}}$ that there exist $a,b \in A$ such that $b=\gamma \cdot a$ and $a \neq 0$.
    Clearly,  $\gamma \cdot (-a)=-b$ holds as well. Since ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$ is totally ordered, we can assume without loss of generality that $a > 0$.
    By the observation, this implies that for each $j \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$, $q_j \cdot a \leq b$ and $b \leq r_j \cdot a$. But since $a,b \in A$ and $a > 0$, this is a counterexample to the validity of rule $\ensuremath{\mathrm{(str_\gamma)}}$ in ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$. By Lemma~\ref{l:about nabla-forms}, $\ensuremath{\mathrm{(str_\gamma)}}^\lor$ fails in ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$ as well. This shows ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$ is not a model of ${\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm {rAb}}}}+\ensuremath{\mathrm{(str_\gamma)}}^\lor$.

label: c:manyEXT
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{c:manyEXT}
There are $2^{2^\omega}$ infinitary extensions of Abelian logic between $\vDash_\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{R}}}}}$ and $\vDash_\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Q}}}}}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
It is a well-known result that the transcendence degree of $\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{R}}}}}$ over $\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Q}}}}}$ is $2^\omega$. From this, it follows that there are $2^{2^\omega}$ distinct subfields of $\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{R}}}}}$ that are field extensions of $\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Q}}}}}$. We argue that the $\ell$-group reduct of each such field is a model of a different infinitary extension of ${\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm {Ab}}}}$.
Let ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$ and ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{B}}}}$ be the $\ell$-group reducts of two distinct subfields of $\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{R}}}}}$ that are field extensions of $\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Q}}}}}$. Without loss of generality, assume that there is a $\gamma \in A \setminus B$ such that $0 < \gamma$. By Proposition~\ref{p:irrational}, an $\ell$-subgroup of $\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{R}}}}}$ validates the rule $\ensuremath{\mathrm{(str_\gamma)}}^\lor$ if and only if $b=\gamma \cdot a \implies a=0$ for all $a,b$ in the corresponding $\ell$-subgroup. Since ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$ and ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{B}}}}$ are the $\ell$-group reducts of subfields of $\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{R}}}}}$, this condition holds if and only if $\gamma$ is not an element of their respective universes.
Hence we obtain that the rule $\ensuremath{\mathrm{(str_\gamma)}}^\lor$ is valid in ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{B}}}}$ but is not valid in ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$. This shows that $\vDash_{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$ and $\vDash_{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{B}}}}$ are different logics.

title: Definition
body_md:
Let ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$ be an Abelian $\ell$-group. A sequence ${\ensuremath{\langle{a_i}\rangle}}_{i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}}$ of elements of $A$ is \emph{strongly decreasing} if, for each $i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$, there is an $n_{i} \geq 4$ such that:
$$
n_{i} \cdot a_{i+1} \geq  a_i \geq 2 \cdot a_{i+1}. 
$$
We call the sequence {\em trivial} if $a_i = 0$ for each $i$.
head: environment

label: l:strongly,strictly-decreasing
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
To prove the first claim, it suffices to show the strictness. Assume that $a_i=a_{i+1}$ for some $i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$. Then the inequality $a_i \geq 2 \cdot a_{i+1}$ becomes $a_i \geq 2 \cdot a_i$ and thus $0 \geq a_i.$ Since also $a_i \geq 0$, we obtain $a_i=0$. For each $j > i$ we have $a_i \geq a_j \geq 0$, thus we get $a_j=0$ as well. Similarly, for $j < i$, there is an $n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$ such that $n \cdot a_i \geq a_j \geq 0$ and thus again $a_j=0$. Therefore, the sequence ${\ensuremath{\langle{a_i}\rangle}}_{i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}}$ has to be trivial, a contradiction.
    
We will prove the second claim. Let us assume that ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$ is an Archimedean chain and ${\ensuremath{\langle{a_i}\rangle}}_{i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}}$ is a strictly decreasing sequence of positive elements. Without loss of generality, as ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$ is Archimedean, we can assume that ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}} \subseteq \ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{R}}}}}$, by Hölder's Theorem.
We construct a non-trivial strongly decreasing sequence ${\ensuremath{\langle{b_i}\rangle}}_{i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}}$. Set $b_0 > 0$ arbitrarily. We will define the rest of the sequence recursively. Assume that we have already constructed $\ensuremath{\langle{b_i}\rangle}_{i \leq n}$ satisfying the conditions from the definition of a strongly decreasing sequence. Now we want a $b_{n+1}$ such that $0< 2 \cdot b_{n+1}\leq b_n$. 

Since ${\ensuremath{\langle{a_i}\rangle}}_{i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}}$ is a strictly decreasing sequence, it follows that there exists a $j \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$ such that $\frac{a_j}{b_n} \notin \mathbb Z$ (otherwise $\ensuremath{\langle{\frac{a_j}{b_n}}\rangle}_{j \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}}$ would be a strictly decreasing sequence of positive elements in $\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Z}}}}}$, which is not possible). 

Since ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$ is Archimedean, there is a $k \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$ such that $0 \leq a_j -k \cdot b_n < b_n$. Since $\frac{a_j}{b_n} \notin \mathbb Z$, we have $0 \neq a_j -k \cdot b_n$ and thus $0 < a_j -k \cdot b_n < b_n$.
Hence, $$0 < a_j -k \cdot b_n \leq \frac{b_n}{2} \; \text{ or } \; 0 < b_n-(a_j -k \cdot b_n) \leq \frac{b_n}{2}.$$ 
Therefore, we set$$b_{n+1}=\min\{a_j -k \cdot b_n, b_n-(a_j -k \cdot b_n)\}.$$ Clearly, $b_{n+1}>0$ and $2 \cdot b_{n+1}\leq b_n$. The second condition for strong decreasing sequences easily follows from the fact that ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$ is Archimedean. Thus, ${\ensuremath{\langle{b_i}\rangle}}_{i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}}$ is a non-trivial strongly decreasing sequence.

label: ex:independence of Arch
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:independence of Arch}
We will show that there are non-Archimedean chains with strictly decreasing sequences of positive elements and with no non-trivial strongly decreasing sequence. Consider the $\ell$-group $\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Z}}}}} \times_{\text{lex}} \ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Z}}}}}$ from Example~\ref{e:ArchNonArch}. 
First, let us consider the sequence ${\ensuremath{\langle{\ensuremath{\langle{1,-i}\rangle}}\rangle}}_{i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}}$. Clearly, this sequence is strictly decreasing and $\ensuremath{\langle{1,-i}\rangle} >0$ for each $i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$. We show that there is no non-trivial strongly decreasing sequence in $\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Z}}}}} \times_{\text{lex}} \ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Z}}}}}$.

Let us assume that ${\ensuremath{\langle{\ensuremath{\langle{a_i,b_i}\rangle}}\rangle}}_{i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}}$ is a strongly decreasing sequence. Clearly $a_i \geq 0$ for all $i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$ since $\ensuremath{\langle{a_i,b_i}\rangle} \geq 0$. Thus, there has to be a $c \geq 0$ such that $a_i=c$ for infinitely many $i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$. Therefore, there has to be a strongly decreasing subsequence ${\ensuremath{\langle{\ensuremath{\langle{c,d_i}\rangle}}\rangle}}_{i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}}$, where $d_i \in \mathbb Z$ and $c \geq 0$. Fix an arbitrary $i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$. We know that $2 \cdot \ensuremath{\langle{c,d_{i+1}}\rangle} \leq \ensuremath{\langle{c,d_{i}}\rangle}$, thus $2\cdot c \leq c$. This implies $c=0$. 
    
Since ${\ensuremath{\langle{\ensuremath{\langle{0,d_i}\rangle}}\rangle}}_{i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}}$ is a strongly decreasing sequence in $\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Z}}}}} \times_{\text{lex}} \ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Z}}}}}$, the sequence $\ensuremath{\langle{d_{i}}\rangle}$ is strongly decreasing in $\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Z}}}}}$. Therefore, $d_i=0$ for all $i \in  \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$. This shows that ${\ensuremath{\langle{\ensuremath{\langle{c,d_i}\rangle}}\rangle}}_{i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}}$ has to be the trivial sequence and so is ${\ensuremath{\langle{\ensuremath{\langle{a_i,b_i}\rangle}}\rangle}}_{i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}}$ as well.

title: Proposition
body_md: Let ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$ be an Abelian $\ell$-group. Then \ensuremath{\mathrm{(IDC)}} is valid in ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$ iff only the trivial sequence is strongly decreasing in ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First, assume that ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$ has a non-trivial strongly decreasing sequence ${\ensuremath{\langle{a_i}\rangle}}_{i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}}$ and note that w.l.o.g.\ we can assume that $n_i = 4$ for each $i$ (if for some $i$ we have $a_i > 4\cdot a_{i+1}$, expand the sequence by putting $2\cdot a_{i+1}$ in a proper place, and repeat \dots). Let us consider the ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$-evaluation $e$ induced by setting $e(x_i) = a_i$. Clearly, all the premises of \ensuremath{\mathrm{(IDC)}} are valid but we have $e(x_0 \rightarrow \ensuremath{\mathtt{t}}) = - a_0 < 0$ and thus the rule \ensuremath{\mathrm{(IDC)}} is not valid in ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$.

Conversely, assume that the rule \ensuremath{\mathrm{(IDC)}} is not valid in ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$, i.e., we have an evaluation $e$ such that if we set $e(\ensuremath{\varphi}_i) = a_i$ the validity of premises of \ensuremath{\mathrm{(IDC)}} tells us that $4 \cdot a_{i+1} \geq a_{i} \geq 2 \cdot a_{i+1}$, i.e., ${\ensuremath{\langle{a_i}\rangle}}_{i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}}$ is a strongly decreasing sequence and, by the failure of the conclusion of the rule, we have $a_0 > 0$, i.e., the sequence is non-trivial.

title: Example
body_md:
There exist $\ell$-groups in $\ensuremath{\mathbf{P}}(\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Z}}}}})$ which have strictly decreasing sequences of positive elements but lack a non-trivial strongly decreasing sequence.

Consider the Abelian $\ell$-group $\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Z}}}}}^\omega$ and note that the sequence of positive elements $$
\ensuremath{\langle{\ensuremath{\langle{\underbrace{0,\dots,0}_{\text{i-times}},1,1,\dots}\rangle}}\rangle}_{i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}}
$$
is strictly decreasing. However, the previous proposition clearly states that only the trivial sequence is strongly decreasing in 
$\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Z}}}}}^{\omega}$, since $\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Z}}}}}^{\omega} \in \ensuremath{\mathbf{P}}(\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Z}}}}})$, $\ensuremath{\mathbf{P}}(\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Z}}}}}) \subseteq \ensuremath{\mathbf{ISP}}_\omega(\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Z}}}}})$, and \ensuremath{\mathrm{(IDC)}} holds in $\ensuremath{\mathbf{ISP}}_\omega(\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Z}}}}})$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$ be a non-trivial linearly ordered Archimedean Abelian $\ell$-group. We want to show that \ensuremath{\mathrm{(IDC)}} is valid in ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$ if and only if ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$ is isomorphic to $\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Z}}}}}$.
By the previous proposition, \ensuremath{\mathrm{(IDC)}} is valid in ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$ if and only if ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$ has only the trivial strongly decreasing sequence.

Since ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$ is an Archimedean chain, by Lemma~\ref{l:strongly,strictly-decreasing}, having only the trivial strongly decreasing sequence is equivalent to having no strictly decreasing sequence of positive elements.

Thus, it suffices to show that a non-trivial linearly ordered Archimedean $\ell$-group ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$ has no strictly decreasing sequence of positive elements if and only if ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}} \cong \ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Z}}}}}$.

Clearly, $\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Z}}}}}$ has no decreasing sequences of positive elements. To show the other implication, one has to argue that $\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Z}}}}}$ is the only non-trivial linearly ordered Archimedean $\ell$-group with no strictly decreasing sequences of positive elements. We can assume, by Hölder's Theorem, that without loss of generality, $\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Z}}}}} \subseteq {\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}} \subseteq \ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{R}}}}}$ and ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$ is not isomorphic to $\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Z}}}}}$. We have to distinguish two cases.
\begin{enumerate}

\item Let $\zeta \in\mathbb R\setminus \mathbb Q$ be an element of $A$. Without loss of generality we can assume $\zeta>1$. Since $1 \in A$, we can generate recursively the following sequence. We start with $r_0=\zeta$ and $r_1=1$. For $n> 0$, we define $k_n=\lfloor \frac{r_{n-1}}{r_n} \rfloor$ and let $r_{n+1}=r_{n-1}-k_n \cdot r_n$. 
By the properties of division, $0 \leq r_{n+1}<r_n$ for all 
$n \geq 1$. This means that the sequence $\ensuremath{\langle{r_n}\rangle}_{n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}}$ is strictly decreasing. Furthermore, because $\zeta$ is irrational, the ratio $\frac{r_n}{r_{n+1}}$ is irrational for each $n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$. This shows that this algorithm never terminates with a zero remainder; thus, $r_n>0$ for all $n$.

\item ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}} \subseteq \mathbb \ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Q}}}}}$. Since ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$ is not isomorphic to $\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Z}}}}}$, ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$ is not generated by any single element. Thus, for each $0<a_n \in A$, there is a $0<b_n \in A$ such that $a_n$ does not generate $b_n$. If $b_n<a_n$ we set $a_{n+1}=b_n$; otherwise, we set $k_n=\lfloor \frac{b_{n}}{a_n} \rfloor$ and 
$a_{n+1}=b_n- k_n \cdot a_n$. Thus, we have constructed $0<a_{n+1}<a_n$.
This allows us to build the desired sequence, and therefore we finish the proof.\qedhere
\end{enumerate}

label: l:isomorRQ
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{l:isomorRQ}
Let ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$ be either $\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{R}}}}}$ or $\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Q}}}}}$ and $a,b \in A\setminus\{0\}$. Then, ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}_a$ and ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}_b$ are isomorphic iff $a \cdot b > 0$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: If $\mathbf{A}_a$ and $\mathbf{A}_b$ are isomorphic, the isomorphism must preserve the underlying natural order, which trivially forces the designated units $a$ and $b$ to have the same sign; hence $a \cdot b > 0$. For the other direction, assume $a \cdot b > 0$. Then $\frac{b}{a} > 0$, and the mapping $h\colon x \mapsto \frac{b}{a} \cdot x$ is an order-preserving group automorphism mapping $a$ to $b$, providing the needed isomorphism.

label: p:varietyZ
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{p:varietyZ}
For any $a,b \in \mathbb{Z}$, we have $\ensuremath{\mathbf{HSP}}(\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Z}}}}}_a)=\ensuremath{\mathbf{HSP}}(\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Z}}}}}_b)$ if and only if $a=b$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
One direction is obvious. To prove the converse one, let us assume $a \neq b$. To show that $\ensuremath{\mathbf{HSP}}(\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Z}}}}}_a) \neq \ensuremath{\mathbf{HSP}}(\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Z}}}}}_b)$, it is sufficient to find an equation which is valid in one of the generating algebras, $\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Z}}}}}_a$ or $\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Z}}}}}_b$, but not in the other.
    If $a<0$ and $b \geq 0$ take the equation $\ensuremath{\mathtt{f}} \geq 0$. This equation clearly holds in $\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Z}}}}}_b$ but it does not hold in $\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Z}}}}}_a$.
    The case $a \leq 0$ and $b>0$ is similar.
    Therefore, it remains to check the cases where $a,b>0$ or $a,b<0$.
    We will check only the first case (the second one is analogous).
    Moreover, let us assume without loss of generality that $0 <a<b$.
     
    Consider the following equation: 

    \begin{equation*} \tag{*}
        (a \cdot x -\ensuremath{\mathtt{f}}) \lor (-x) \geq 0.
    \end{equation*}
    This equation is not valid in $\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Z}}}}}_b$, since if we take an evaluation $e$ such that $e(x)=1$ we get $(a \cdot e(x) -b) \lor (-e(x))=(a-b) \lor -1 < 0$. Thus the equation (*) does not hold in $\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Z}}}}}_b$.
    
    We show the same equation holds in $\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Z}}}}}_a$. First let us consider an evaluation $e$ such that $e(x) \leq 0$. Clearly, we get $-e(x) \geq 0$ and thus $(a \cdot e(x) - a) \lor e(-x) \geq 0.$  
    It remains to consider an evaluation $e$ such that $e(x)>0$ (and thus $e(x) \geq 1$). Then $a \cdot e(x) -a \geq a \cdot 1-a=0$. Thus the equation (*) is valid in $\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Z}}}}}_a$.

label: l:similar extensions
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The implications from 1 to 2 and from 1 to 3 are clear (note that in the second case we need to use linearity of ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$ to obtain that if $\ensuremath{\mathtt{f}}^{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}} \not\geq 0$ and $\ensuremath{\mathtt{f}} \vee \ensuremath{\varphi} \geq 0$, then $\ensuremath{\varphi} \geq 0$). We prove the converse ones at once by contradiction:
assume that $\ensuremath{\mathtt{f}} \vDash_{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}} \varphi$ (resp.\ that  $\ensuremath{\mathtt{f}}\vee \varphi \vDash_{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}} \varphi$)
and $\ensuremath{\mathtt{f}}^{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}} \geq 0$. For an arbitrary element $a$ and any evaluation $e(\varphi) = a$, the premises of both rules are trivially valid and so we obtain $a \geq 0$, a contradiction with the assumption that ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}} \neq {\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{1}}}}$.

label: t:Lu completeness
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{t:Lu completeness}
$\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm {Lu}}}$ is finitely strongly complete with respect to any of the following sets of algebras: $\{\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{R}}}}}_{-1}\}$, $\{\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Q}}}}}_{-1}\}$, and $\{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}_{a} \mid a < 0\}$ for any non-trivial Abelian $\ell$-group ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We prove the final part of the claim, the rest then follows from Lemma~\ref{l:isomorRQ}. Using Theorem~\ref{t:pAb lots R} and Corollary~\ref{c:ultra-decomposition of semilinear logics}, we know that 
$$
\mathbf{Alg}^{\ell}(\ensuremath{\mathrm \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm {Lu}}}}) \subseteq \mathbf{Alg}^{\ell}(\ensuremath{\mathrm {\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm {pAb}}}}}) \subseteq \mathbf{I}({\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{1}}}}) \cup \ensuremath{\mathbf{ISP}}_\mathrm{U}(\{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}_{a} \mid a < 0\}) \cup \ensuremath{\mathbf{ISP}}_\mathrm{U}(\{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}_{a} \mid a \geq 0\}).
$$
Clearly, for any non-trivial element of $\ensuremath{\mathbf{ISP}}_\mathrm{U}(\{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}_{a} \mid a \geq 0\})$, we have $\ensuremath{\mathtt{f}}^{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}_{a}}\geq 0$ (an equation preserved by ultrapowers) and thus it is not a member of $\mathbf{Alg}^{\ell}(\ensuremath{\mathrm \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm {Lu}}}})$ due to the previous lemma. Thus 
$$
\mathbf{Alg}^{\ell}(\ensuremath{\mathrm \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm {Lu}}}}) \subseteq \mathbf{I}({\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{1}}}}) \cup \ensuremath{\mathbf{ISP}}_\mathrm{U}(\{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}_{a} \mid a < 0\})
$$
and so the proof is done by Corollary~\ref{c:ultra-decomposition of semilinear logics}.\qedhere

title: Definition

label: t:LU completeness
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{t:LU completeness}
The logic $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm {Lu}}}_{\infty}$ is strongly complete with respect to $\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{R}}}}}_{-1}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Corollary~\ref{c:semilinearity_criterium}, the logic $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm {Lu}}}_{\infty}$ is semilinear.
Since $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm {Lu}}}_{\infty}$ is an expansion of ${\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm {rAb}}}}$, every linearly ordered $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm {Lu}}}_{\infty}$-algebra is a pointed Archimedean $\ell$-group. Since $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm {Lu}}}_{\infty}$ is an extension of $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm {Lu}}}$, by Lemma~\ref{l:similar extensions}, we know that in any non-trivial ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$ linearly ordered $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm {Lu}}}_{\infty}$-algebra we have $\ensuremath{\mathtt{f}}^{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}} < 0$. Thus, ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$ has to be a pointed Archimedean $\ell$-group with a negative point $a$. Thus, by Hölder's Theorem~\cite{Holder:Axiome}, there is an embedding $h$ of the $\ensuremath{\mathtt{f}}$-free reduct of ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$ into $\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{R}}}}}$. Clearly $h$ can be seen as an embedding of ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$ into $\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{R}}}}}_{h(a)}$. As 
$h(a) < 0$, we know that  $\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{R}}}}}_{h(a)}$ is isomorphic to $\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{R}}}}}_{-1}$ (Lemma~\ref{l:isomorRQ}). Therefore, 
$\mathbf{Alg}^{\ell}(\ensuremath{\mathrm \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm {Lu}}}_{\infty}}) \subseteq \ensuremath{\mathbf{IS}}(\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{R}}}}}_{-1})$. Since $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm {Lu}}}_{\infty}$ is semilinear and $\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{R}}}}}_{-1}$ is an $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm {Lu}}}_{\infty}$-algebra it follows that $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm {Lu}}}_{\infty}$ is strongly complete with respect to $\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{R}}}}}_{-1}$.

label: t:LukLUtranslation
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{t:LukLUtranslation}
Let $\Gamma \cup \{\ensuremath{\varphi} \}$ be a set of formulas. Then, we have
$$
\Gamma \vdash_{{\mathchoice{\mbox{\rm\L}}{\mbox{\rm\L}}{\mbox{\rm\scriptsize\L}}{\mbox{\rm\tiny\L}}}_\infty} \ensuremath{\varphi} \qquad\text{ iff }\qquad \tau[\Gamma]\vdash_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm {Lu}}}_\infty} \tau(\ensuremath{\varphi}) .
$$
Moreover, if $\Gamma$ is finite we have
$$
\Gamma\vdash_{{\mathchoice{\mbox{\rm\L}}{\mbox{\rm\L}}{\mbox{\rm\scriptsize\L}}{\mbox{\rm\tiny\L}}}} \ensuremath{\varphi} \qquad\text{ iff }\qquad \tau[\Gamma]\vdash_{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm {Lu}}}} \tau(\ensuremath{\varphi}) .$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Recall that, thanks to the known completeness properties, we can replace the syntactical consequence relations by semantical ones w.r.t.\ algebras ${\mathchoice{\mbox{\bf\L}}{\mbox{\bf\L}}{\mbox{\bf\scriptsize\L}}{\mbox{\bf\tiny\L}}}$ and ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm {Lu}}}}}}}$ (because it is an isomorphic copy of $\ensuremath{{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{R}}}}}_{-1}$).

Let us consider any mapping $e$ of propositional variables into reals and
define the mapping $\bar e$ as its restriction to $[0,1]$, i.e., 
$$
\bar e(p) = 
\begin{cases}
     e(p) & \text{ if } e(p) \in [0,1] \\
     1    & \text{ if } e(p) \geq 1 \\
     0    & \text{ if } e(p) \leq 0.
\end{cases}
$$
We denote by $(\bar e)^{\mathchoice{\mbox{\bf\L}}{\mbox{\bf\L}}{\mbox{\bf\scriptsize\L}}{\mbox{\bf\tiny\L}}}$ and $e^{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Lu}}}}$ the corresponding evaluations. By a simple proof by induction over the complexity of formula $\ensuremath{\chi}$, we obtain:
$$
(\bar e)^{\mathchoice{\mbox{\bf\L}}{\mbox{\bf\L}}{\mbox{\bf\scriptsize\L}}{\mbox{\bf\tiny\L}}}(\ensuremath{\chi}) = e^{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Lu}}}}(\tau(\ensuremath{\chi})).
$$
Clearly, it holds for variables and constants by definition of $\bar e$ and $\tau$. 
Now assume $(\bar e)^{\mathchoice{\mbox{\bf\L}}{\mbox{\bf\L}}{\mbox{\bf\scriptsize\L}}{\mbox{\bf\tiny\L}}}(\alpha) = e^{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Lu}}}}(\tau(\alpha))$ and $(\bar e)^{\mathchoice{\mbox{\bf\L}}{\mbox{\bf\L}}{\mbox{\bf\scriptsize\L}}{\mbox{\bf\tiny\L}}}(\beta) = e^{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Lu}}}}(\tau(\beta))$ for formulas $\alpha,\beta$. We want to show that $(\bar e)^{\mathchoice{\mbox{\bf\L}}{\mbox{\bf\L}}{\mbox{\bf\scriptsize\L}}{\mbox{\bf\tiny\L}}}(\alpha \circ \beta) = e^{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Lu}}}}(\tau(\alpha \circ \beta))$ for $\circ \in \{\land,\lor,\ensuremath{\mathbin{\&}},\rightarrow\}$. We show this step only for $\circ=\ensuremath{\mathbin{\&}}$.
We write:
\begin{multline*}  
    e^{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Lu}}}}(\tau(\alpha \ensuremath{\mathbin{\&}} \beta))=e^{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Lu}}}}((\tau(\alpha) \ensuremath{\mathbin{\&}} \tau(\beta)) \lor \ensuremath{\mathtt{f}})=  (e^{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Lu}}}}(\tau(\alpha))+e^{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Lu}}}}(\tau(\beta))-1) \lor 0= \\ ((\bar e)^{\mathchoice{\mbox{\bf\L}}{\mbox{\bf\L}}{\mbox{\bf\scriptsize\L}}{\mbox{\bf\tiny\L}}}(\alpha)+(\bar e)^{\mathchoice{\mbox{\bf\L}}{\mbox{\bf\L}}{\mbox{\bf\scriptsize\L}}{\mbox{\bf\tiny\L}}}(\beta)-1) \lor 0=(\bar e)^{\mathchoice{\mbox{\bf\L}}{\mbox{\bf\L}}{\mbox{\bf\scriptsize\L}}{\mbox{\bf\tiny\L}}} (\alpha \ensuremath{\mathbin{\&}} \beta).
\end{multline*}


Now we can prove the left-to-right direction of the first equivalence. Assume that $\Gamma\vDash_{{\mathchoice{\mbox{\bf\L}}{\mbox{\bf\L}}{\mbox{\bf\scriptsize\L}}{\mbox{\bf\tiny\L}}}} \ensuremath{\varphi}$ and that $e$ is a mapping such that for each $\gamma\in \Gamma$ we have (recall that $\ensuremath{\mathtt{t}}^{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{LU}}}} = 1$)
$$
e^{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Lu}}}}(\tau(\gamma)) \geq 1.
$$
As $e^{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{Lu}}}}(\tau(\gamma)) = (\bar e)^{\mathchoice{\mbox{\bf\L}}{\mbox{\bf\L}}{\mbox{\bf\scriptsize\L}}{\mbox{\bf\tiny\L}}}(\gamma)$ we have
$(\bar e)^{\mathchoice{\mbox{\bf\L}}{\mbox{\bf\L}}{\mbox{\bf\scriptsize\L}}{\mbox{\bf\tiny\L}}}(\gamma) = 1$ for $\gamma\in\Gamma$ and so, by the assumption, also
$(\bar e)^{\mathchoice{\mbox{\bf\L}}{\mbox{\bf\L}}{\mbox{\bf\scriptsize\L}}{\mbox{\bf\tiny\L}}}(\ensuremath{\varphi}) = 1$, which entails $e^{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm {Lu}}}}}}}(\tau(\ensuremath{\varphi})) = 1$.

To prove the converse direction, it suffices to note that if the co-domain of $e$ is a subset of $[0,1]$, then $e = \bar e$. 

The second equivalence can either be proved in exactly the same way or actually follows from the first one and the fact that on finite sets of premises the \L ukasiewicz (unbound) logic coincides with its infinitary variant.

title: Lemma
body_md:
Let ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}} \in \mathbf{Alg}^{\ell}(\ensuremath{\mathrm {\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm {pAb}}}}})$ and ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}} \neq {\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{1}}}}$. Then:
\begin{itemize}
\item $\ensuremath{\mathtt{f}}^{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}} < 0$ iff the rule $\ensuremath{\mathtt{f}} \lor \ensuremath{\varphi} \mathrel{\blacktriangleright} \ensuremath{\varphi}$ is valid in ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$.

\item $\ensuremath{\mathtt{f}}^{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}} \neq 0$ iff the rule $(\ensuremath{\mathtt{f}}\wedge -\ensuremath{\mathtt{f}}) \lor \ensuremath{\varphi} \mathrel{\blacktriangleright} \ensuremath{\varphi}$ is valid in ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$.
\item $\ensuremath{\mathtt{f}}^{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}} \geq 0$ iff the axiom $\mathrel{\blacktriangleright} \ensuremath{\mathtt{f}}$ is valid in ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$.
\item $\ensuremath{\mathtt{f}}^{\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}} > 0$ iff the rule $-\ensuremath{\mathtt{f}} \lor \ensuremath{\varphi} \mathrel{\blacktriangleright} \ensuremath{\varphi}$ is valid in ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$.
\end{itemize}

title: Proof
body_md:
Consider an arbitrary ${\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}_a$-evaluation $e_1\colon\ensuremath{\mathit{Fm}_{\!\ensuremath{\mathcal L_{{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm {pAb}}}}}}}} \longrightarrow {\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}_a$. Clearly, $e_1$ extends the evaluation $e_0\colon\ensuremath{\mathit{Fm}_{\!\ensuremath{\mathcal L_{{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm {Ab}}}}}}}} \longrightarrow {\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}$. Clearly there is a unique evaluation $e_2\colon\ensuremath{\mathit{Fm}_{\!\ensuremath{\mathcal L_{{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm {pAb}}}}}}}} \longrightarrow {\ensuremath{\boldsymbol {\mathit{A}}}}_{-a}$ extending $e_0$ such that $e_1(\ensuremath{\mathtt{f}})=-e_2(\ensuremath{\mathtt{f}})=e_2(-\ensuremath{\mathtt{f}})$ and $e_1(x)=e_2(x)$ for all variables $x$. By induction one can show that $e_1(\ensuremath{\psi}) =e_2(\tau(\ensuremath{\psi}) )$ for each formula $\ensuremath{\psi} \in \ensuremath{\mathit{Fm}_{\!\ensuremath{\mathcal L_{{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm {pAb}}}}}}}}$.
Therefore, $e_1(\ensuremath{\psi}) \geq 0$ iff $e_2(\tau(\ensuremath{\psi}) ) \geq 0$. From this, one can easily derive the statement of this theorem.
